idiom_name: Predef.identity[A](x: A): A — the auto-imported stdlib identity
implementation_notes: Scala ships the identity function in the standard library: Predef.identity[A](x: A): A is auto-imported into every compilation unit via Predef and documented as 'a method that returns its input value', so the classic structure is not hand-written at all — the neutral element is available unqualified wherever a Function1 slot exists (names.map(identity), people.groupBy(identity)), and Function1's own compose/andThen carry the composition law: f.compose(identity) and identity.andThen(f) behave as f. Because Predef.identity is a method, passing it as a value eta-expands it to a Function1 (automatic in Scala 3, expected-type-driven or `identity _` in Scala 2), and the direct call is eliminated by the compiler — the 2.13 Scaladoc annotates identity with @inline. The hand-rolled form def id[A](a: A): A = a stays justified only for specialized cases: a JVM-SAM-typed function value with a specific signature, hoisting one monomorphic instance per type in a hot path, or Scala.js/Scala Native targets where the generic Function1 wrapper shows up in emitted size.
pitfalls: identity is a method on object Predef, not a stable Function1 value: every eta-expansion site (`identity _` in Scala 2, or a bare `identity` forced to function type) can allocate a fresh wrapper object, and a generic polymorphic val is impossible — hoist one monomorphic instance per type (e.g. val idF: String => String = identity) in hot paths instead of re-expanding at each call site.

The @inline on Predef.identity only eliminates the call when it is applied directly; passed through a non-inlined Function1 boundary (stored in a List, returned from a factory, handed to a Java consumer) the JVM still performs a virtual apply, and Scala.js/Scala Native may not inline at all — do not assume zero overhead in latency-critical pipelines without measuring.

sortBy(identity) compiles whenever the element type already has an Ordering and silently sorts by the whole element — a forgotten key derivation hides behind the natural order instead of failing; likewise map(identity) and groupBy(identity) look like tautologies yet build new collections sharing element references — pass-through is not a defensive copy, so downstream mutation of the elements is visible to the original.

identity propagates exceptions unchanged: Try(x).map(identity) or an identity stage in a Future/IO chain does not rescue a missing error-handling strategy; and writing bare identity where a value is expected (e.g. println(identity)) prints the function object instead of calling it — in Scala 2 the bare reference even fails to compile without a function-typed expected type or an explicit identity _.
